items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A recurring element that develops a theme"?
items.answer: motif
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of motif.

items.stem: Distinguish between a subject and a theme.
items.answer: A subject is what the novel is about (war); a theme is what it suggests about the subject (war destroys the moral certainties of those who fight).
items.markingKey: A subject is what the novel is about (war); a theme is what it suggests about the subject (war destroys the moral certainties of those who fight). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why expressing a theme as a statement is better than a single word.
items.answer: A statement ("power corrupts those who fear weakness") is arguable and specific, guiding analysis better than a topic word. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A statement ("power corrupts those who fear weakness") is arguable and specific, guiding analysis better than a topic word. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a novel (an original extract written for study).

Margit checked the oven again. Six o'clock. He had said six. The table was set for two, the good glasses out, the candles not yet lit – no point lighting candles for nobody. Of course he would be late; he was always late, and she always forgave him, and that was the arrangement, wasn't it? She lit the candles anyway. Let them burn.

Explain how a symbol in this extract could develop a theme across a whole novel.
items.answer: The candles symbolise hope and romance, then time passing and defiance; "Let them burn" suggests both waste and refusal to wait.
items.markingKey: The candles symbolise hope and romance, then time passing and defiance; "Let them burn" suggests both waste and refusal to wait. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). Identification without effect: half marks at most.

items.stem: "A novel has one theme that the author intends." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Novels usually explore several interconnected themes, and readers may interpret them differently.
items.markingKey: Novels usually explore several interconnected themes, and readers may interpret them differently. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the following fan fiction based on Jane Austen's 'Pride and Prejudice' (an original extract written for study).

Charlotte Lucas did not love Mr Collins. She had never expected to. What she loved, she discovered in the first week at Hunsford, was the small sitting room at the back of the parsonage, where he never came because the light was poor. There she read, and wrote letters to Elizabeth, and was, for two hours each afternoon, nobody's wife.

What thematic concern does this extract introduce, and how might a novel develop it?
items.answer: Women, marriage and economic security. Supporting feature: "nobody's wife" (climactic phrase) – the ending reveals the freedom Charlotte values.
items.markingKey: Women, marriage and economic security. Supporting feature: "nobody's wife" (climactic phrase) – the ending reveals the freedom Charlotte values. Credit any well-justified alternative supported by the text; the answer given is the most direct reading.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Character is the main vehicle of theme in the novel."
items.answer: Character is a central vehicle but works with structure, voice and motif.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: characters' choices dramatise ideas; readers connect to themes through people. Arguments against: setting, structure and narrative voice also carry theme; motifs develop meaning independently. Supported judgement: Character is a central vehicle but works with structure, voice and motif.

items.stem: Trace the development of one theme across a novel you have studied, referring to its opening, a central episode and its ending.
items.answer: Indicative content: thematic statement; three stages; authorial methods; evaluation of development.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: thematic statement; three stages; authorial methods; evaluation of development.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a novel narrated in the first person (an original extract written for study).

I want to be clear that I did not take the money. I borrowed it, which is different, and I would have returned it on Friday if Friday had gone the way Fridays usually go. Anyone would have done the same. Ask anyone. Ask my brother – no, don't ask my brother; he has always exaggerated.

Explain how a symbol in this extract could develop a theme across a whole novel.
items.answer: The money is less a symbol than a test of the narrator's honesty.
items.markingKey: The money is less a symbol than a test of the narrator's honesty. items.stem:
Read the following extract from a memoir (an original extract written for study).

I remember the kitchen as yellow. My sister insists it was green, and she has the photographs to prove it. But I have kept it yellow for forty years, because yellow is the colour of the morning my father taught me to make bread, and I am not ready to give that morning back.

How does the extract suggest that memory is unreliable or selective?
items.answer: The memoirist admits that her memory is factually wrong but emotionally true, showing that memoir constructs the self through selective, emotionally shaped memory rather than objective record.

items.stem:
Read the following infographic from an international water charity, described in words.

[Title in bold blue capitals: 'THE WALK'.] [A single dotted line runs right across the page and ends at a small well icon.]
Label beside the line: 'The distance many women and girls in rural areas walk for water each day: up to 6 km.'
Below: '20 litres. That's what she carries back – about the weight of a full suitcase.'
[Bottom panel: a tap icon.] 'A donation of 25 euros helps bring a tap within 15 minutes of her home.'

Apply a feminist lens to this text: how does it represent gender and power?

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a short novel translated from Spanish (an original passage written for study).

The señora paid Rosa on Fridays, in cash, counting each note aloud as if Rosa might not know her numbers. Rosa had taught three of the señora's children to read. She said nothing. She folded the money twice and put it in her shoe, where the señora's eyes did not follow.

Read this extract through a feminist or Marxist lens: what does it reveal about power?
items.answer: Class power is shown through the employer's condescending ritual of counting aloud; the irony that Rosa taught the children to read exposes the injustice; hiding the money in her shoe is a small act of private control.
items.markingKey: Class power is shown through the employer's condescending ritual of counting aloud; the irony that Rosa taught the children to read exposes the injustice; hiding the money in her shoe is a small act of private control. items.stem:
Read the following opinion column in a weekend newspaper.

To scroll or not to scroll: that is the question every teenager answers two hundred times a day. Whether 'tis nobler to endure the slings and arrows of the group chat, or to take arms against a sea of notifications and, by switching off, end them. Most of us, adults included, choose the scroll. Hamlet at least had the excuse of a ghost.

Explain what this text borrows from an earlier text and what it changes.
items.answer: The column parodies Hamlet's soliloquy ("To be, or not to be ... the slings and arrows of outrageous fortune ... take arms against a sea of troubles"); its humour depends on recognising the source.

items.stem:
Read the following fan fiction based on Jane Austen's 'Pride and Prejudice' (an original extract written for study).

Charlotte Lucas did not love Mr Collins. She had never expected to. What she loved, she discovered in the first week at Hunsford, was the small sitting room at the back of the parsonage, where he never came because the light was poor. There she read, and wrote letters to Elizabeth, and was, for two hours each afternoon, nobody's wife.

Explain how this text transforms its source.
items.answer: The piece borrows Austen's characters and the detail, present in the novel, that Charlotte prefers a back room her husband avoids; it shifts focalisation from Elizabeth to Charlotte, giving a minor character inner life and reframing her pragmatic marriage as a search for private freedom.

items.stem:
Read the following poem 'Penelope' (an original poem written for study).

Penelope

Twenty years I wove and unwove,
and they called it faithfulness.
No one asked what I was making
in the hours the loom stood still –
a self, thread by thread,
that no returning king could wear.

How does this text respond to an earlier work?
items.answer: The poem rewrites Homer's Odyssey, in which Penelope weaves a shroud by day and unravels it by night to delay her suitors while Odysseus is away for twenty years; it gives her a voice and reinterprets the weaving as self-making rather than wifely loyalty.
items.markingKey: The poem rewrites Homer's Odyssey, in which Penelope weaves a shroud by day and unravels it by night to delay her suitors while Odysseus is away for twenty years; it gives her a voice and reinterprets the weaving as self-making rather than wifely loyalty. Read the following ending of a short story (an original extract written for study).

For eleven years Mr Okafor had walked past the music shop on Calle Real without stopping. Today the violin in the window had a small handwritten sign: 'Played by a beginner. Still learning.' He stood there until the shopkeeper came out, and then, to his own surprise, he went in.

What thematic concern does this extract introduce, and how might a novel develop it?
items.answer: Fear, ageing and second chances. Supporting feature: "'Played by a beginner. Still learning.'" (epiphany) – the sign triggers a sudden insight that permits change.

Read the following extract from a novel translated from Arabic (an original passage written for study).

In my father's house, the men ate first. My mother called this respect. My aunt, who had studied law in Cairo before her marriage, called it nothing at all; she simply ate standing in the kitchen doorway, her plate in one hand and a newspaper in the other, so that she belonged to neither room.

items.answer: The family meal ritual encodes male precedence; the mother accepts it as "respect", while the educated aunt resists silently by occupying the threshold – the doorway symbolises her position between tradition and independence.

items.answer: Updating the setting tests whether the source's concerns still apply, makes it accessible and can expose how power or prejudice persists.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a memoir (an original extract written for study).

I remember the kitchen as yellow. My sister insists it was green, and she has the photographs to prove it. But I have kept it yellow for forty years, because yellow is the colour of the morning my father taught me to make bread, and I am not ready to give that morning back.

Express a theme suggested by this extract as a statement and explain the evidence for it.
items.answer: Memory, truth and the construction of the self. Supporting feature: "I remember the kitchen as yellow. My sister insists it was green" (contrast) – the conflict between memory and evidence foregrounds the reliability of memoir.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Unreliable narrators make readers better readers."
items.answer: They reward and develop attentive reading, though their effect depends on the reader.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: they demand active inference; they train attention to clues. Arguments against: some readers miss the unreliability; they can frustrate. items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Applying modern critical lenses to older novels is unfair to them."
items.answer: It is fair if done with awareness of context: the aim is understanding, not condemnation.
